newsitem.title: FINLAND: Environmental image growing issue for metal miners.
newsitem.headline: Environmental image growing issue for metal miners.

text.p: Regulation and public opinion on environmental issues are a growing consideration in the mining industry, mining officials said at the Metal Bulletin base metal concentrates conference on Wednesday.

The president of Finland's Outokumpu Base Metals Oy, Asko Ojanen, said the mining industry had to promote itself better as well as act responsibly and improve technology -- or suffer the consequences in the marketplace.

"The image of the industry has to be restored. We have to compete equally against other products and industries, which until now have been more successfully promoted as eco-friendly," Ojanen told delegates.
"If we fail to understand this and to respond sympathetically, the consequences ... may even prevent us from operating and bring an end to mine development and expansion projects," he said.
In recent times, hotly-debated topics included the use of nickel in coins for the European Union, the use of copper in roofing and plumbing and the use of zinc and zinc alloys, he added.

Boliden Ltd's president and CEO Anders Bulow said in another presentation that the mining industry had actually come a long way in improving environmental standards -- even more so than regulators required in some cases.

"Although new environmental legislation being introduced in many of the 'new' mining countries is very stringent, growing competition to attract investment makes it tempting for newly industrialised countries to relax environmental standards," Bulow said, calling for the industry to insist on high standards.
Recycling metals might be one way the industry could improve public acceptance, he added.

Boliden's Ronnskar copper smelter in Sweden had changed its raw materials base over the years and now more than 30 percent of copper production, 40 percent of gold production and nearly 90 percent of zinc production derived from various forms of scrap, he said.
However, Bulow criticised the European Union's Basel Convention for applying what he called unrealistic limits on the movement of scrap metals.
"In some instances it is the mining industry that is leading the way while regulators become mired in bureaucratic details of their own making," he said.
